# Multiple alignment and trees

Five species carry a version of *BRCA1*: human, chimpanzee, mouse, dog and
chicken. All five coding sequences sit in
`data/sequences/brca1_cds_five_species.fasta`. Their lineages split apart in
some order, and inside that file the differences between the sequences are the
only record of it. Can you get the order back out of the letters? And when a
program hands you an order, what would tell you it's wrong?

## A column has to mean the same thing five times

In Chapter 18 you lined two sequences up. Each column held two letters and made
one small claim: these two bases correspond.

Five sequences make that claim ten times over in a single column, once for
every pair you can pick out of five. A column now says all five of these bases
sit at the same position in the same ancestral gene. Human against
mouse might want a gap in one spot, and human against dog might want it three
bases along. A [multiple sequence alignment]{.term def="One alignment of three
or more sequences, in which every column makes a single claim about all of them
at once."} has to pick one arrangement and hold it for every pair in the set.

Here's the first 60 columns of the one Clustal Omega returned. I've dropped the
running position count that the real file prints at the end of every row, so
the block fits this page.

``` {.default filename="data/alignment/brca1_cds_five_species.aln"}
human           ATGGATTTATCTGCTCTTCGCGTTGAAGAAGTACAAAATGTCATTAATGCTATGCAGAAA
chimpanzee      ATGGATTTATCTGCTCTTCGCGTTGAAGAAGTACAAAATGTCATTAACGCTATGCAGAAA
mouse           ATGGATTTATCTGCCGTCCAAATTCAAGAAGTACAAAATGTCCTTCATGCTATGCAGAAA
dog             ATGGATTTATCTGCGGATCGTGTTGAAGAAGTACAAAATGTTCTTAATGCTATGCAGAAA
chicken         ATGGACTTGTCAGTGATTGCCATTGGAGACGTGCAAAATGTGCTTTCAGCCATGCAGAAG
                ***** ** ** *         **  *** ** ********  **   ** ********
```

Read it down, not across. The bottom line is the conservation line, and it
carries a `*` under every column where all five sequences hold the same letter
and a space everywhere else. Column 1 is `A` five times. Columns 1 to 3 are the
start codon `ATG`, which is where a coding sequence begins in all five.

Now look at the run of stars near the right-hand end. The last nine columns are
`ATGCAGAAA` in human and `ATGCAGAAG` in chicken. Eight of the nine are
conserved and the ninth isn't, which is exactly what the conservation line
shows.

Nothing here computed the best possible arrangement of five sequences. That
can't be done for anything past a few short ones, so an aligner takes a
shortcut. It gets a rough idea of which sequences resemble which, aligns the
closest ones first, then brings the rest in against what it has built so far.
The ordering comes from a quick tree the program builds for itself. That tree
is called a [guide tree]{.term def="A rough tree an aligner builds to decide
what order to align sequences in. It is a scheduling device."}. It exists to
schedule the work, and none of it is meant as a claim about history. Keep it
apart from the tree Clustal hands back when the run finishes. Those are two
different objects, and this chapter turns on the difference.

## Gaps make the alignment longer than anything that went into it

Sixty columns further on, at column 121, the alignment runs into a length
difference.

<!-- nlr-allow: 121 -->

``` {.default filename="data/alignment/brca1_cds_five_species.aln"}
human           CACATATTTTGCAAATTTTGCATGCTGAAACTTCTCAACCAGAAGAA---AGGGCCTTCA
chimpanzee      CACATATTTTGCAAATTTTGCATGCTGAAACTTCTCAACCAGAAGAA---AGGGCCTTCA
mouse           CACATATTTTGCAAATTTTGTATGCTGAAACTTCTTAACCAGAAGAA---AGGGCCTTCA
dog             CACATATTTTGCAAATTTTGTATGCTGAAACTTCTCAACCAGAGGAA---GGGGCCTTCA
chicken         CACGTATTCTGCAGATTCTGTATGTTTAAACTTCTCAGCAGAAAGAAAAAAGGTGTAATA
                *** **** **** *** ** *** * ******** * *   * ***    **      *
```

Four species have three dashes where chicken has `AAA`. A dash isn't a letter
in the sequence. It's the alignment saying this species has nothing at this
position, and it costs a column that four of the five sequences never needed.

The alignment can't tell you which way that happened. Chicken may have gained
three bases, or the common ancestor of the four mammals may have lost them.
Both stories produce the same picture, which is why the honest word for it is
an *indel* rather than an insertion or a deletion.

A column like that one makes the whole alignment wider than any sequence that
went into it. Read the file in and count the dashes. The file has one row per
species per block, and each of those rows starts with a letter, so that's the
test for whether a line is sequence. One other line starts with a letter too,
`CLUSTAL O(1.2.4)` at the top of the file, which is why the code below throws
that one out by name.

```{python}
rows = {}
for line in open("data/alignment/brca1_cds_five_species.aln"):
    if line[:1].isalpha() and not line.startswith("CLUSTAL"):
        name, chunk, position = line.split()
        rows[name] = rows.get(name, "") + chunk

for name in rows:
    gaps = rows[name].count("-")
    print(f"{name:11} {len(rows[name])} columns  {gaps} gaps  "
          f"{len(rows[name]) - gaps} bases")
```

Every row is 5,838 columns wide, because every row has to be. The longest
coding sequence that went in was the dog's at 5,637 bases, and the alignment is
201 columns longer than that.

::: {.check}
Subtract each species' gap count from 5,838 and you get the length of the
sequence that went in. Dog: 5,838 − 201 = 5,637. Human: 5,838 − 246 = 5,592.
Chicken: 5,838 − 588 = 5,250. If one of yours doesn't land on a length from
Chapter 5 or from the FASTA file, your parser picked up a line it shouldn't
have.
:::

Now count the columns where all five agree. `zip` is the one from Chapter 18,
widened: it hands you the five letters at position 0, then the five at position
1, and so on down the alignment.

```{python}
columns = list(zip(*rows.values()))

identical = 0
for column in columns:
    if len(set(column)) == 1 and "-" not in column:
        identical += 1

print(identical, "of", len(columns), "columns are identical in all five")
print(round(100 * identical / len(columns), 1), "percent")
```

<!-- nlr-allow: 1787 -->

Under a third of the gene survives unchanged across all five species. That's
the number a conservation line is showing you, one screen at a time.

## Running this yourself

EMBL-EBI runs Clustal Omega as a public service. There's no account to make and
nothing to install. You paste FASTA into a box, tell it the sequences are DNA
rather than protein, and start the job. The five coding sequences together come
to 28 kilobytes of text.

<!-- nlr-allow: 28 -->

Coding sequence, not mRNA. The untranslated ends of an mRNA aren't conserved
between a human and a chicken. Put them in and both ends of the alignment fill
up with columns that say nothing about the gene.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live EMBL-EBI Clustal Omega service on 2 August 2026. Form
labels move. Three things have to be on that form under some name: the box you
paste sequences into, the choice between DNA and protein, and the control that
starts the job. On that date the service built its tree by neighbor joining.
:::

The job queues, and then three results come back: the alignment you've been
reading, a percent identity matrix, and a tree. All three are in
`data/alignment/` in this book's repository, so nothing below depends on the
service being up the evening you read it.

## The identity matrix, and the floor underneath it

The percent identity matrix is the alignment reduced to one number per pair.
Here's the whole of it, with the comment lines at the top of the file dropped.

``` {.default filename="data/alignment/brca1_cds_five_species.pim"}
     1: human       100.00   99.28   73.18   83.90   49.25
     2: chimpanzee   99.28  100.00   73.36   84.04   49.17
     3: mouse        73.18   73.36  100.00   70.65   46.56
     4: dog          83.90   84.04   70.65  100.00   49.34
     5: chicken      49.25   49.17   46.56   49.34  100.00
```

<!-- nlr-allow: 46.56 49.34 73.36 84.04 49.17 -->

Read the human row across. Chimpanzee comes in at 99.28 percent, dog at 83.90,
mouse at 73.18 and chicken at 49.25. One row down, mouse to dog is 70.65.

Stop on those two numbers for a second. Dog is closer to human than mouse is,
by 83.90 − 73.18 = 10.72 percentage points. The gap isn't relatedness. NCBI
Taxonomy groups mouse with human and chimpanzee and leaves the dog outside, and
a later section here has you check that yourself. What the number reports is
how much change has piled up, and change piles up faster in some lineages than
in others.

There's also a floor under the whole table that nothing on the page mentions.
DNA has four letters. Two sequences with no relationship at all still agree at
about one column in four, because a quarter is what random agreement between
four letters looks like: 100 ÷ 4 = 25. So the 49.25 between human and chicken
is 24.25 points above pure chance, and the 46.56 between mouse and chicken is
closer to the floor still.

::: {.why}
The reason anyone builds a tree from a single gene is to answer a question
about identity. You find a *BRCA1*-like sequence in an organism nobody has
studied. Is it the same gene doing the same job, or a copy that split off long
ago and drifted into something else? The branching order is the evidence, so
getting the branching order wrong changes the biological claim you end up
making.
:::

## A tree written as text

The tree comes back as one string of names and punctuation, closed by a
semicolon. This format is called [Newick]{.term def="A text format for trees.
Parentheses group, commas separate, a colon and a number give a branch length,
and a semicolon ends the tree."}, and it's what tree software reads and writes.
Clustal breaks the string across lines wherever it likes. Here it is rewrapped
into three so the grouping shows.

``` {.default filename="data/alignment/brca1_cds_five_species.phylotree"}
((human:0.00399,chimpanzee:0.00316):0.07035,
 (mouse:0.15374,chicken:0.38062):0.04650,
 dog:0.08637);
```

Parse it by hand, from the inside out. Four rules cover everything in it.

1. A name is a leaf. `dog` is one sequence.
2. A colon and a number after a name is the length of the branch leading to
   that leaf.
3. A pair of parentheses groups whatever is inside it, and the colon and number
   after the closing parenthesis belong to the branch leading to that group.
4. The semicolon ends the tree.

So `(human:0.00399,chimpanzee:0.00316)` is a group of two, and the `:0.07035`
after it is the branch that group hangs from. `(mouse:0.15374,chicken:0.38062)`
is a second group of two. Then `dog:0.08637` sits on its own.

Count the commas at the top level. There are two, so the outermost parentheses
hold three items, not two. A tree with a root has exactly two things at the
top, because a root is one split into two. Three items is Newick's way of
saying this tree is unrooted. There's no oldest node in it, so it carries no
direction of time and no answer to which lineage came off first. What the tree
still claims is which sequences group with which.

Branch lengths are estimated substitutions per site. Human's branch is 0.00399
and chimpanzee's is 0.00316, so the distance between them along the tree is
0.00399 + 0.00316 = 0.00715, or about 0.7 changes per hundred columns.

::: {.check}
Check that against the identity matrix. It puts human and chimpanzee at 99.28
percent identical, so they differ at 100 − 99.28 = 0.72 percent of columns. The
tree says 0.715 and the matrix says 0.72. Both numbers came off the same
alignment, so this tells you your reading of the tree is right. It does not
tell you the tree is right. If the two disagree by more than a rounding step,
you added the wrong branches together.
:::

## Distances or likelihood

There are two families of method for turning an alignment into a tree, and the
difference between them matters for the rest of this chapter.

A distance method throws the alignment away and keeps one number per pair,
exactly like the matrix above. Then it looks for the tree whose branch lengths
best reproduce those numbers. It's fast and it scales, which is why an aligner
uses one for its guide tree.

Maximum likelihood keeps every column. You give it a model of how bases change
over time, and it asks which tree makes this exact alignment most probable. It
scores one candidate tree after another. It's far slower on the same sequences,
and it uses evidence a distance method throws away, including which base
changed into which.

Here's what one number per pair can't hold. It cannot tell "this site changed
once" apart from "this site changed three times and landed back on the letter
it started with". Over a short branch the difference is small. Over a long one
it isn't, and the distance comes out too low. Published phylogenies mostly use
maximum likelihood or a Bayesian method for that reason.

So which kind is the tree in `data/alignment/`? Clustal Omega built two trees
on this job. The first was the guide tree, and its work was over before the
alignment existed. The second is the one you were handed: a tree built by a
distance method from the finished alignment, which is what the EMBL-EBI service
produces by default. Nothing in the file names the method, and nothing in it
warns you a distance was involved.

One more thing is missing. A published tree normally carries a support number
on each internal branch. Here's how you get one. Build a fresh alignment the
same width as the real one by drawing its columns at random, with the same
column allowed to come up twice. Make a tree from that. Do the whole thing a
few hundred times. A branch's support number is the percentage of those trees
that contained it. The procedure is called the *bootstrap*, and those
percentages are the numbers you see sitting on the branches of a published
tree. A branch that survives nearly every resample is a different claim from
one that survives half of them. Go back and count the support numbers in the
Newick block. There are none.

This book doesn't run a maximum-likelihood program, because doing it properly
means picking a substitution model and defending the choice, and that's a
chapter this book doesn't have. What you can do without one is read the tree
you were given and check it against something outside itself. That's the rest
of this chapter.

## The tree groups a mouse with a chicken

Take the topology on its own and compare it against NCBI Taxonomy, the
classification NCBI hangs on every sequence record. NCBI assembles it from the
published systematics literature rather than ruling on it, and none of the five
placements below is in dispute. Human and chimpanzee are Primates, inside
Euarchontoglires, inside Mammalia. Mouse is Rodentia, inside
Euarchontoglires, inside Mammalia. Dog is Carnivora, inside Laurasiatheria,
inside Mammalia. Chicken is Aves. All five are Tetrapoda.

Four mammals and one bird, then. The computed tree pairs the mouse with the
chicken.

That isn't a subtle disagreement. Mouse shares a clade with human and
chimpanzee that dog doesn't share, and chicken is outside all four. The
grouping the tree reports puts a rodent and a bird together, to the exclusion
of three other mammals. Rooting won't rescue it. A root only puts a direction
on branches that are already there. This tree has a branch with mouse and
chicken on one side and human, chimpanzee and dog on the other. Taxonomy needs
mouse on the same side as the primates, and no tree does both.

The cause is in the branch lengths, and you already have them. Mouse's branch
is 0.15374. Chicken's is 0.38062. Every other number in that file is under
0.09. The two primates only look short because they share a stem, so add
human's two numbers to get from human out to the middle of the tree: 0.00399 +
0.07035 = 0.07434. Still under 0.09. Those two are the fastest-changing
sequences in the set, and it isn't close.

Now put that together with the floor under the identity matrix. A long branch
means many changed sites. DNA has four letters. When a site changes on two
separate branches, there's a real chance both landed on the same letter, and
the alignment shows a match that neither species inherited. The faster a branch
runs, the more of these accidental matches it manufactures. Two fast branches
manufacture them with each other.

Mouse and chicken read 46.56 percent identical against a chance floor of 25.
A distance method has no way to separate the accidental matches from the
inherited ones. It reads the accidents as evidence and pulls the two longest
branches toward each other. That effect has a name: *long-branch attraction*.
Joseph Felsenstein worked out the conditions for it in 1978. It's why the two
fastest-changing sequences in a small set are the ones most likely to come out
as neighbors when they shouldn't.

::: {.trap}
A tree always has a shape. Every branch in that file carries a length, printed
to five decimal places, and not one of them carries a confidence. Nothing marks
the grouping the data supports least. The output of a wrong tree and the output
of a right tree are the same kind of object. If you hadn't checked this one
against NCBI Taxonomy, you'd have had no reason to doubt it.
:::

## What an outgroup is for

An [outgroup]{.term def="A sequence you are confident sits outside the group
you are studying, added to a tree so the rest of it can be oriented."} is a
sequence you add on purpose, chosen because you're already sure it falls
outside everything else in the set. It gives the tree something to be oriented
against. The branch leading to the outgroup is where the root goes, and every
other branch takes a direction from that.

Frog is the obvious one here. `NM_001114491.1` is the *Xenopus tropicalis* copy
of the gene, and its coding sequence is 4,779 bases. NCBI writes that symbol
`brca1`, all lowercase, which is a third convention on top of the two Chapter 5
gave you. NCBI Taxonomy puts frog in Amphibia, inside Tetrapoda, so it sits
outside the birds and outside the mammals both.

The six-sequence alignment and its tree are already in `data/alignment/`, under
the name `brca1_cds_with_outgroup`. Don't open them yet. Exercise 19.2 asks you
to write down what you think the frog will do before you look, and the
prediction is most of the exercise.

## One gene isn't a species tree

Everything in this chapter came off one gene. Suppose the method were perfect
and the alignment were perfect. The tree for a gene can still differ from the
tree for the species carrying it. Two copies of a gene in two living species
can trace back to a common ancestor older than the split between those
species. When that happens the gene keeps a history of its own.

That's why a published phylogeny uses many genes at once, and it's why a
disagreement between a one-gene tree and NCBI Taxonomy isn't automatically a
bug. The reasoning runs in an order, though. Check the method first. Grouping a
rodent with a bird to the exclusion of three mammals is not a story about
*BRCA1*, and the branch lengths told you which explanation to reach for.

Test them against the other three. Human's distance to the middle of the tree

0.08637. Both of your numbers should be bigger than all three of those. If one
isn't, you've picked a branch that isn't long, and long is the whole
explanation.

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/alignment/brca1_cds_five_species.aln'"}
Python is speaking, and it's looking in the folder your notebook is standing
in. Chapter 15 covered this: a path with no slash in front of it gets read from
where you are. If your copy of the alignment sits next to the notebook, change
the path to `"brca1_cds_five_species.aln"` and nothing else in the cell
changes.
:::

::: {.errfix err="ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 3, got 2)"}
Python is speaking, and it's counting fields. Each row of the file should be a
name, a chunk of sequence and a running position, which is three. Yours has
two, so you downloaded the alignment in a format that leaves the position count
off. Either take the numbered Clustal format or change that line to
`name, chunk = line.split()`.
:::

::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 'Human'"}
Python is speaking. The keys in `rows` come from the FASTA headers you sent to
the aligner, and those are lowercase. `rows['Human']` isn't `rows['human']`,
and a dictionary won't guess. Print `list(rows)` to see the five names you
actually have.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Your column count isn't 5,838 and your identity numbers don't match the ones printed here"}
Nothing broke. You aligned something else. The usual cause is aligning the full
mRNA records instead of their coding sequences, which drags the untranslated
ends into the comparison and moves every number on the page. Check the length
of what you submitted: the human coding sequence is 5,592 bases and the human
mRNA is 7,088.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}

- Say why a five-way alignment has more columns than the longest sequence in it
- Recover each input length from the alignment by subtracting that species' gaps
- Name the grouping in the five-species tree that contradicts NCBI Taxonomy, and
  the two branch lengths behind it
- Explain why two fast-changing sequences get pulled together by a distance
  method
- Say what an outgroup did to this tree and name the one error it left in place
:::
